extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, and law students studying patent re-issues
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and limits governing when and how a patent may be re-issued: what may or may not be added, omitted, or changed (elements, sub-combinations, species/genera, process steps, apparatus, product), and timing/procedural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue void if omits an essential element
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue of a combination patent is void if it omits one of the essential elements of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), Neacy v. Allis (1882), Gammeyer v. Newton (1879), Redmond v. Parham (1879). A re-issue that drops an essential element departs from the original and cannot be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substitution of different element unless mere equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: That the re-issue of a combination-patent cannot substitute another element for one of those contained in the original, unless the substituted element be a mere equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalents may be introduced by the re-issue provided their equivalence is pointed out in the re-issued specification. See Blackman v. Kibbler (1879), Gill v. Wells (1874), National Spring Co. v. Union Car Spring Mfg. Co. (1874).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot omit element because later deemed unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: That the re-issue of a combination-patent cannot omit one of the elements on the ground that experience has shown it to be unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases Hale v. Stimpson (1865), Vance v. Campbell (1861). Omitting an element merely because later shown unnecessary is not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot re-issue a combination as a different/lower combination
rubrics_metrics.description: That an original covering a combination of four elements cannot re-issue as covering three only, or the combination of three with a different fourth element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gill v. Wells (1874) and related cases: re-issue must not make a new combination distinct from the original combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue void when it constitutes a different combination operating differently
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue is void when the original was for a combination and the re-issue is for another combination, containing only part of the elements of the former and operating in a different way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson v. Railroad Co. (1882) and related authorities: re-issue must be for the same invention; mere partial overlap with different operation invalidates re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of formerly essential element expands the Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: That when an element formerly claimed as essential is omitted, the Claim is expanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips v. Risser (1885): omission of an essential element broadens the scope and is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bound by solicitor's description of essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: That if an inventor allows his solicitor to describe an element as essential and the patent so issues, he is bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original patent describes an element as essential and it issues that way, the inventor cannot escape that characterization in a re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue lawful if actual nature of combination unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: If the actual nature of the combination is unchanged the re-issue may vary widely from the original in its statement of the invention as well as in its Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-essential parts erroneously described may be omitted; equivalents may be introduced if equivalence is pointed out in the re-issue specification. (See Treatise discussion and Gill v. Wells (1874)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essential features may be omitted in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue of a combination-patent may omit one or more of the non-essential features described in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perham v. American Buttonhole, Overseaming & Sewing Machine Co. (1871) and other cases permit omission of non-essential parts; but if such features were claimed as essential, mistake may be irremediable (see §§ 278, 282, 527 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: If non-essential was claimed as essential, mistake may be irremediable
rubrics_metrics.description: That if non-essential features were, however, claimed as an essential element the mistake is irremediable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to earlier sections indicate that where the original claim treated a non-essential part as essential and it was claimed as such, the error cannot (necessarily) be cured by re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where original describes two equivalent elements, re-issue may claim either alone
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the original patent describes and claims two elements, either of which is the equivalent of both, the re-issue may claim either alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donbar v. White (1881) and related authorities: where elements are equivalents, individual claiming in re-issue is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issued combination may embrace sub-combinations shown in original
rubrics_metrics.description: When the original patent describes and claims only the combination, but substantially sets forth any or all of the various sub-combinations in model, drawings, or specifications, these may be claimed in the re-issue, if not before abandoned or disclaimed, provided they originated from the inventive genius of the same inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christman v. Rumsey (1879), The Com Planter Patent, Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), and others support claiming sub-combinations that were sufficiently indicated in the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may claim sub-combinations even if language differs
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue need not describe sub-combinations in the exact language of the original, but may contain a more full and exact description of the same invention; identity of sub-combination as to elements and cooperative law must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A re-issue for sub-combinations is sustained when the original indicated those sub-combinations as practically operative and the re-issue indicates how each may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness supports re-issue for sub-combinations (six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the sub-combinations claimed in the re-issue were shown in the original and the re-issue is applied for within six months after the grant of the original, inadvertence or mistake need not be specially proved; the speedy application is sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jenkins v. Stetson (1887), 82 Fed. Rep. 398: speedy application (within six months) creates presumption supporting re-issue claims for sub-combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may embrace individual elements of a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a patent for a combination may embrace such of its essential elements as are substantially indicated in the original specification, drawings, or model, and were the inventions of the same inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every element of a combination is an operative means and may be a distinct invention; re-issue can secure exclusive use of each separately claimed element if adequately indicated originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot change essential character of an element
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue cannot depart from the original as to the essential character therein given to the element; if the original treats one form of the element as necessary to its performance in the combination, the re-issue must adhere to that form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where form was material in the original description, re-issue cannot broaden to all forms. See examples referencing Matthews v. Machine Co. and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: When form not material, re-issue may claim all forms or restrict to one member of a class
rubrics_metrics.description: But when form is not made material by the original description, the re-issue may claim all forms of the element; or when the original describes an element as consisting in a class of acts or substances, the re-issue may confine the element to any single member of that class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gong Bell Mfg. Co. v. Clark (1878); St Louis Stamping Co. v. Quinby (1879) provide illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim new groupings not described as sub-combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to bring individual elements within the operation of the patent by re-issue does not authorize the inventor to claim in it any grouping of elements which the original did not describe as a sub-combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue must respect groupings/sub-combinations that were indicated in the original; inventing new groupings in re-issue is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot reclaim an element disclaimed (except by mere mistake)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any individual element has been disclaimed, unless by mere mistake, the combination-patent cannot be re-issued to reclaim it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers made (not by mistake) are binding; re-issue cannot reverse a deliberate disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements shown only as connected portions in drawings cannot be later claimed as inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements shown in the original drawings only as a connected portion of the mechanism, and so described, cannot be claimed on the re-issue as an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ives v. Sargent (1887) and related authority: mere depiction as part of larger mechanism is not sufficient to later claim that part as separate invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot cover separate elements after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination-patent cannot re-issue to cover the separate elements after unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archer v. Amd (1887), Bantz v. Frantz (1882): undue delay in seeking separate-element claims can bar re-issue for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic/species relation limits re-issue (generic may embrace one species)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the re-issue of a generic patent, the species which the original describes and which might have appropriately been claimed therein may be protected; but if the specification of the original generic patent describes two or more species, one only can be claimed in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generic invention is distinct from each species; only one species may be joined with the genus in a single patent; Joinder rules and limitations discussed (JBe parte McClintock etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific patent cannot re-issue to claim the genus (except narrow exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a specific invention cannot re-issue to embrace the generic; exception: where inventor described and claimed the genus in his application but was compelled (without fault) to accept a patent for the specific invention alone, he may amend to insert the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue cannot be used to expand a specific patent to cover the whole genus unless original application circumstances justify it (see Ex parte Waters, Ex parte Ewart, and Treatise discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of a process/art must be confined to same acts and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a patent for an art or process must be confined to the same acts and operations which constitute the essential features of the original invention. No new act can be added; no former operation described and claimed as necessary can be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Middlings Purifier Co. v. Atlantic Milling Co. (1879) and related authorities: process re-issue is constrained to original essential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of a process may omit steps if process remains substantially same
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a patent for a process may omit some of the steps described in the original, if the process remains substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Wooten (1872) indicates allowable omissions where the substantive character of the process is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of a process cannot add a new step
rubrics_metrics.description: That the re-issue of a patent for a process cannot add a new step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Middlings Purifier Co. v. Atlantic Milling Co. (1879) and similar decisions: adding steps amounts to new matter and is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may substitute a material of same class used before application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an original, in describing a process, mentioned one material which does not answer the purpose, the re-issue may describe another material of the same class which will serve the same desired end, if it had been used by the inventor before his original application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Mayall (1873): substitution is allowed only if inventor had used the substitute prior to the original application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and apparatus/product relations determine whether re-issue may claim apparatus or product
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the art itself, the re-issue may in certain cases cover the apparatus it employs or the product in which it results, where these were invented by the same inventor, sufficiently described originally, and neither abandoned nor disclaimed; the right depends on their relation to the art and the propriety of joining them in the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the process cannot be performed without the apparatus mentioned, or the product uniformly follows employment of the process, the inventions are inseparably connected and re-issue may cover product or apparatus (Treatise discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot add apparatus/process not originally indicated (machine vs process)
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine-patent cannot be re-issued to include a process which consists in the mere use of the machine, nor a process in which the patented machine performs a necessary though subordinate part; such processes lie outside the scope of a patent originally confined to the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 675 discussion: the function (use) of a machine is not itself patentable subject matter under a machine patent unless properly indicated and joined originally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of machine (non-combination) limited to same parts or equivalents under same structural law
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue of a patent for a machine, if the machine be not a combination, must be limited to the same parts or their equivalents associated under the same structural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue may vary mechanical adaptations and cover any mode of using the machine properly indicated in the former specification, but cannot change the structural law of the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot cover product and process unless both substantially described
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue cannot cover a product and a process unless both have been substantially described in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penn. Salt Mfg. Co. v. Thomas (1871) and other cases: both product and process need substantial original description to be claimed in re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original limited to product by one process cannot re-issue to cover product by other process
rubrics_metrics.description: An original patent confined to a product produced by one process only cannot re-issue to cover the product produced by another process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacuum Oil Co. v. Buffalo Lubricating Oil Co. (1884) and analogous decisions: re-issue cannot broaden to new process routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue for product void if original was for process unless process always results in product
rubrics_metrics.description: That a re-issue for a product is void where the original was for the process, unless the use of the process always results in the product, and thus both are one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powder Works v. Powder Co. (1878) and discussion: product claims deriving from a process-patent require that the process necessarily produces the product.
